verses.text: When Saul’s son heard that Abner was dead in Hebron, his hands became feeble, and all the Israelites were troubled.

Saul’s son had two men who were captains of raiding bands. The name of one was Baanah, and the name of the other Rechab, the sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, of the children of Benjamin (for Beeroth also is considered a part of Benjamin:
and the Beerothites fled to Gittaim, and have lived as foreigners there until today).

Now Jonathan, Saul’s son, had a son who was lame in his feet. He was five years old when the news came about Saul and Jonathan out of Jezreel; and his nurse picked him up and fled. As she hurried to flee, he fell and became lame. His name was Mephibosheth.
The sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, Rechab and Baanah, went and came at about the heat of the day to the house of Ishbosheth, as he took his rest at noon.
They came there into the middle of the house, as though they would have fetched wheat; and they struck him in the body: and Rechab and Baanah his brother escaped.
Now when they came into the house, as he lay on his bed in his bedroom, they struck him, killed him, beheaded him, and took his head, and went by the way of the Arabah all night.

They brought the head of Ishbosheth to David to Hebron, and said to the king, “Behold, the head of Ishbosheth, the son of Saul, your enemy, who sought your life! Yahweh has avenged my lord the king today of Saul, and of his offspring. ”
David answered Rechab and Baanah his brother, the sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, and said to them, “As Yahweh lives, who has redeemed my soul out of all adversity,
when someone told me, ‘Behold, Saul is dead,’ thinking that he brought good news, I seized him and killed him in Ziklag, which was the reward I gave him for his news.
How much more, when wicked men have slain a righteous person in his own house on his bed, should I not now require his blood from your hand, and rid the earth of you?”

David commanded his young men, and they killed them, cut off their hands and their feet, and hanged them up beside the pool in Hebron. But they took the head of Ishbosheth, and buried it in Abner’s grave in Hebron.

footnotes.content: Abner's death is a turning point—the kingdom trembles. Fear unmakes us when we've leaned on the wrong strength. Only when our hands go feeble do we learn to reach for the Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Two captains of raiders—men who lived by the sword, now ready to move. Names matter in Scripture; these men's deeds will speak louder than their offices ever could. The Lord sees those who work in the shadows.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Beeroth and Gittaim—two places woven together by flight and exile. The Beerothites lived as foreigners in a foreign land, carrying their displacement into the author's present day. Sometimes home is not a place we return to, but a promise we hold.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A child's accident in a moment of chaos—one tumble that changes a life's whole arc. Mephibosheth's lameness is not his shame; it is a mark of survival, a story he carries. The Lord often meets us in brokenness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Noon rest, the heat of the day—a moment when the mind is drowsy and the guard is lowered. Evil often works in plain daylight, hiding in the ordinary rhythms of a man at ease. Nothing takes the Lord by surprise.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Pretense masks intent—they came as if to buy grain, but carried murder in their hearts. How often we hide our true selves behind a show of purpose. Deception is the thief of trust.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Beheading and flight through the night—an act so violent it can only have been seized by ambition. They thought they were building a kingdom; they were only adding blood to their own hands.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They bring their trophy to David, certain their crime will be reward. How little they know the man before them—a man the Lord has taught that justice and mercy are not the same thing. Evil thinks it speaks the language of the victors.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "As Yahweh lives"—David swears by the living God, not by power or circumstance. He is answering with his faith, declaring his allegiance even in a moment of judgment. The heart that fears the Lord speaks first.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David remembers the man who brought word of Saul's death and claimed credit—he died in Ziklag for that ambition. David does not reward the trophy of a man's death; he will never purchase the throne with blood.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "A righteous person in his own house"—Ishbosheth may have been weak, a puppet, but he was defenseless. There is a covenant that protects the vulnerable in their beds. The Lord's justice reaches into the most hidden rooms.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo in this: David's refusal to accept blood-bought favor, and his swift judgment of those who brought it. In a world that rewards the cut-throat, the Lord still honors those who refuse the offer of unclean hands. Looking back from where we stand, we see how rare this was—and how rare it remains.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
